content: Heart disease and stroke can be managed or prevented through specific lifestyle changes. These include reducing stress, consuming a diet low in fat and salt, losing weight if overweight, engaging in regular physical activity, and quitting smoking. To help prevent dementia, it is beneficial to keep your mind active with mental exercises such as reading or solving crossword puzzles. For promoting healthy bones, lifestyle modifications include increasing weight-bearing exercises, avoiding smoking, limiting alcohol consumption, and eating a well-balanced diet rich in calcium and vitamin D. If you miss a dose of your medication, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is close to the time of your next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular schedule. Do not double the dose to catch up. Store medications at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Avoid storing them in the bathroom. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Properly discard expired or unused medications. Always consult your healthcare professional for complete information about the medication and your specific health needs. Estrogens, whether used alone or with another hormone (progestin), have been associated with rare but serious side effects. These include an increased risk of uterine cancer (endometrial cancer), which can be reduced by taking progestin as directed by your doctor. In postmenopausal women, estrogens, with or without progestin, may increase the risk of breast or ovarian cancer, stroke, dementia, and serious blood clots. The risk of these side effects may depend on the dose and duration of estrogen use. This medication should be used at the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration necessary. Regularly discuss the use of this medication with your doctor and have periodic check-ups (e.g., every 3 to 6 months) to determine if continued use is necessary. If long-term use is required, annual physical exams, including breast exams, mammograms, pelvic exams, and Pap smears, are recommended. This medication is a hormone (estrogen) used by women to alleviate menopause symptoms such as hot flashes and vaginal dryness, which occur due to decreased estrogen production. Certain estrogen products may also be used postmenopause to prevent bone loss (osteoporosis). However, other medications like raloxifene or bisphosphonates (e.g., alendronate) may be safer and equally effective for preventing bone loss. Take this medication by mouth, with or without food, as directed by your doctor. If using extended-release tablets, do not crush, chew, or dissolve them, as this can release the drug all at once, increasing the risk of side effects. Take the medication regularly at the same time(s) each day to maximize its benefits. Follow your dosing schedule carefully. Common side effects may include stomach upset, nausea, vomiting, bloating, breast tenderness, headache, or weight changes. Remember, this medication has been prescribed because your doctor believes the benefits outweigh the risks. Rarely, this medication may cause serious, potentially fatal blood clot-related problems, such as heart attack, stroke, or clots in the lungs or legs. Severe allergic reactions to this product are rare. Before taking this medication, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it or have any other allergies. This product may contain inactive ingredients that could cause allergic reactions or other issues. Avoid smoking or using tobacco while on this medication, as it increases the risk of blood clots. Inform your doctor if you have recently had or will undergo surgery, or if you will be confined to a chair or bed for an extended period (e.g., during a long flight), as these conditions increase the risk of blood clots, especially when taking estrogen products. If you are nearsighted or wear contact lenses, you may experience vision problems or difficulty wearing your lenses. Children may be more sensitive to the side effects of this drug, potentially affecting their growth and development. This medication should not be used during pregnancy. It passes into breast milk and may reduce the quality and quantity of milk produced. Discuss with your doctor if you are breastfeeding. Drug interactions may alter how your medications work or increase the risk of serious side effects. Keep a list of all the products you use (including prescription, nonprescription, and herbal products) and share it with your doctor and pharmacist. This medication may interfere with certain lab tests (e.g., metyrapone test), potentially causing false results. In case of overdose with serious symptoms such as passing out or difficulty breathing, call 911 immediately. Otherwise, contact a poison control center. U.S. residents can call 1-800-222-1222, and Canadian residents can call 1-844-764-7669. Lifestyle changes such as reducing stress, eating a low-fat/low-salt diet, losing weight if overweight, exercising regularly, and quitting smoking are essential. Additionally, keeping your mind active with mental exercises like reading or solving puzzles can help prevent dementia. To promote healthy bones, engage in weight-bearing exercises, avoid smoking, limit alcohol intake, and consume a balanced diet with adequate calcium and vitamin D.
